structure.overview: This case concerns an appeal by Finastra International Limited against the decision of a trademark officer regarding the use and registration of the FENESTRAE mark owned by Fenestrae B.V., a Dutch software company. The officer partially upheld the registrations related to Faxination and Udocx software and services, deleting some goods and services due to lack of evidence of use in Canada. The Federal Court allowed the appeal in part, finding no palpable error in the officer's findings on Faxination but identifying palpable and overriding error regarding the evidence of use for Udocx services, resulting in partial success for the appellant and no order as to costs.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Respondent Fenestrae BV is a Dutch software company owning the FENESTRAE mark, with a subsidiary in Georgia providing support and sales.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Respondent uses the FENESTRAE mark mainly for Faxination, a secure digital document platform, and Udocx, a cloud-based document conversion solution.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The Officer grouped registered goods/services by product and upheld only some registrations; the Appellant wants all goods/services deleted.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The appeal is allowed in part for reasons explained below.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Mr. Hogewoning admitted the mark was unused in Canada for some hardware goods, which were deleted accordingly.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Faxination was described broadly but established as at least computer facsimile software with modular components.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The Officer divided goods into Computer Facsimile Software and Remaining Computer Software Goods classes.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Computer Facsimile Software included software for transmission and analysis of various media across networks.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: No evidence showed Faxination exchanged audio or moving pictures, so those entries were deleted.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Appellant argued no evidence showed software installation images were viewed in Canada; some indicated Netherlands accounts.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Officer found FENESTRAE mark on installation images sufficient to associate the mark with Faxination subscription.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Remaining Computer Software Goods included backup hard drives and various peripherals and software for payment processing.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Officer agreed backup hard drives lacked sales evidence and deleted these goods accordingly.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Mr. Hogewoning's description of backup hard drives was unsupported; Officer found no association with the mark.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: No evidence supported credit card software goods; general references were deleted.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Officer found Faxination descriptions matched registered telecommunication and facsimile messaging services.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Audio and moving pictures were not described for Faxination and were deleted from services.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Officer found Faxination subscription included performance of related services, supported by promotional materials.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Udocx described as cloud-based document conversion correlated with registered cloud computing and access services.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Despite no Udocx subscriptions, Officer accepted advertising and availability in Canada during relevant period.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Brochures showed FENESTRAE and UDOCX as distinct marks, each with its own registered symbol.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Officer did not infer Udocx backorders meant availability but accepted direct sales and display of goods/services with mark.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Remaining services not addressed in affidavit were deleted by the Officer.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Questions of fact and mixed fact-law are reviewed for palpable and overriding error; questions of law for correctness.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Decision on evidence interpretation is overturned only for palpable and overriding error, meaning obvious and outcome-affecting error.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Court must decide if Officer made palpable and overriding errors in drawing inferences from the evidence as a whole.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Court finds no adverse inference justified as Respondent does not contest factual deficiencies found by Officer.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Officer found Respondent's evidence sufficient; Appellant bears burden to show palpable and overriding error for expungement.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Appellant argues invoices with Canadian addresses lacked shipping costs and no proof goods arrived in Canada.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Sale qualifies as normal trade if genuine arm's length transaction; burden is low and may be inferred by Officer.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Justice Nadon in JC Penney explained that a single genuine sale can prove trademark use in the normal course of trade, excluding token or related-party sales.
idea_list: definition of normal course of trade

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: No evidence suggested Mr. Hogewoning's transactions were outside the normal course of trade; the Officer properly relied on the documents and explanations.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Nothing indicated the sales in Exhibit D were not genuine commercial transactions or excluded types; Respondent only needed to show genuine sales pattern.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Respondent needed only a prima facie case; Officer could reasonably infer delivery from invoices to major clients with shipping addresses.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Officer reasonably inferred Exhibit D's Nestlé invoice related to Exhibits A and C's Faxination software from a holistic evidence assessment.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Officer accepted Mr. Hogewoning's statement that the installation screen image was viewed in Canada; no reason to think it differed from the Netherlands.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Officer found the Respondent showed use of Faxination goods based on affidavit and exhibits, deleting goods lacking use evidence; no palpable error found.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Appellant argues invoices and affidavit descriptions don't prove registered services were performed in Canada; ordering isn't use under s 4(2).

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The term 'services' is liberally construed; services are performed if persons in Canada derive tangible benefit during the relevant period.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Officer found Faxination services performed and Udocx services at least advertised and available in Canada during the relevant period.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Officer reasonably inferred Faxination services were performed from evidence including annual subscription invoices to institutional clients.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Appellant notes Udocx licenses were backordered, suggesting services weren't available during the relevant period.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Officer rejected the Appellant's 'tacit admission' claim, finding Udocx was sold directly and the backorder notice may postdate the relevant period.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: No evidence beyond Mr. Hogewoning's assertion showed Udocx use in Canada; mere assertion without evidence is insufficient.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Under s 45, proof burden is light but evidence must show use within three years and not be bald assertions.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Respondent needed factual assertions showing use of Udocx services; Officer erred by accepting bald assertion and only advertising evidence.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Officer committed palpable and overriding error by finding Udocx services used during the relevant period without sufficient evidence.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Because the appeal's success is divided, no order as to costs will be made.
